query: Which dependence-robust inference methods (block permutation, wild-cluster bootstrap, Driscoll–Kraay) best address cross-sectional and calendar clustering in our panel?

response.query: Which dependence-robust inference methods (block permutation, wild-cluster bootstrap, Driscoll–Kraay) best address cross-sectional and calendar clustering in our panel?
response.answer: Driscoll–Kraay standard errors best address cross-sectional and calendar clustering in panel data. Block permutation and wild-cluster bootstrap are also robust methods for such data.

results.title: Robust Standard Errors for Panel Regressions with Cross-Sectional Dependence
results.content: Section 3 describes the xtscc program that produces Driscoll and Kraay standard errors for coefficients estimated by pooled OLS /weighted least-squares (WLS ) regression and FE (within) regression. Furthermore, estimating the covariance matrix with this approach yields standard errors that are robust to general forms of cross-sectional and temporal dependence. assumptions are met, we know little about how well standard error estimates per-form when the residuals and the explanatory variables of large-scale microeconometric panels are cross-sectionally and temporally dependent. Although there are both studies that address the consequences of spatial and temporal dependence explicitly 6 and stud-ies that consider medium- and large-scale panels, 7 I know of no analysis that investigates the small-sample properties of standard error estimates for large-scale panel datasets with spatially dependent cross-sections. By comparing the coverage rates from several techniques of estimating (robust) standard errors for linear panel models, I can replicate and extend Driscoll and Kraay’s original finding that cross-sectional dependence can lead to severely biased standard error estimates if it is not accounted for appropriately. Even though coverage rates of Driscoll and Kraay standard errors are typically below their nominal value, Driscoll and Kraay standard errors have considerably better small-sample properties than those of commonly applied alternative techniques for estimating standard errors when cross-sectional dependence is present. For OLS , White, Rogers, and Newey–West standard errors’ cross-sectional correlation leads to coverage rates that are far below their nominal value, irrespective of whether regression model ( 5) is estimated by pooled OLS or FE regression. The results of the reference simulation discussed in the last section suggest that the small-sample properties of Driscoll–Kraay standard errors outperform those of other (more) commonly used covariance matrix estimators when cross-sectional dependence is present. Although being somewhat superior when there is no spatial dependence, coverage rates of OLS and Rogers standard errors in figure 4 are clearly dominated by those of the Driscoll–Kraay estimator when cross-sectional correlation is present. Regression ( 10 ) should therefore be estimated with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors since they are robust to general forms of cross-sectional and temporal dependence. However, when the residuals are cross-sectionally correlated, then the aforemen-tioned covariance matrix estimators lead to severely downward-biased standard error estimates for both pooled OLS and FE (within) regression.

results.title: Driscoll and Kraay: Significance and symbolism
results.content: # Significance of Driscoll and Kraay. Driscoll and Kraay standard errors are used in panel data regressions to address potential biases arising from cross-sectional dependence. The Driscoll and Kraay estimation model manages heteroscedasticity and serial correlation issues. It employs a nonparametric covariance matrix estimator that assumes spatial and temporal independence. Synonyms: - , Robust standard errors, Panel-corrected standard errors. It is your responsibility to fact check each reference. ## The concept of Driscoll and Kraay in scientific sources Science Books. Driscoll and Kraay addresses biased estimates in panel data regressions caused by cross-sectional dependence, heteroscedasticity, and serial correlation. It uses a nonparametric covariance matrix estimator. (1) The Driscoll and Kraay standard errors estimation model is used to manage the issues of heteroscedasticity and serial correlation, proposing a nonparametric covariance matrix estimator that is spatially and temporally independent. (2) Panel data regressions with the Driscoll and Kraay standard errors are run to overcome any possibility of biased estimates from the cross-sectional dependence problem.

results.title: [PDF] Robust Standard Errors for Panel Regressions with Cross-Sectional ...
results.content: 1–31 Robust Standard Errors for Panel Regressions with Cross-Sectional Dependence Daniel Hoechle University of Basel Abstract. In this paper I present a new Stata program, xtscc, which estimates pooled OLS/WLS and ﬁxed eﬀects (within) regression models with Driscoll and Kraay (Review of Economics and Statistics 80: 549-560) standard errors. By run-ning Monte Carlo simulations, I compare the ﬁnite sample properties of the cross-sectional dependence consistent Driscoll-Kraay estimator with the properties of other, more commonly employed covariance matrix estimators that do not account for cross-sectional dependence. The results indicate that Driscoll-Kraay standard errors are well calibrated when cross-sectional dependence is present. Thereby, I also propose a Hausman-type test for ﬁxed-eﬀects that is robust to very general forms of cross-sectional and temporal dependence. It is the aim of this paper to contribute to this tradition by providing a Stata implementation of Driscoll and Kraay’s (1998) covariance matrix estimator for use with pooled OLS estimation and ﬁxed eﬀects regression.
